_about: Ground station illustration of the Earth link panel (issue #81). Every fact and number below is taken from NASA's official Deep Space Network page (source_url), read on 15 November 2026. Images are Unity renders, not photographs (frontend/public/media/CREDITS.md). Station visibility is computed by /api/earth-link (issue #110), not drawn from these pictures.
intro: NASA's Deep Space Network listens from three complexes: Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. Their placement keeps contact as Earth turns: before a spacecraft sinks below the horizon at one site, another site can pick up the signal.
moon_note: On 20 July 1969, Deep Space Network antennas helped receive the first downlink and two-way communication from the surface of the Moon.
illustration_note: Illustration: these pictures are renders made with Unity. They are not photographs of the real sites.
no_station_note: These pictures are illustrations, not data. Which station sees the Moon is computed in the station cards above, for the Moon's centre rather than for the site; Earth visibility is computed from the landing site for Earth's disk.

globe.alt: Illustration of Earth and the Moon in space, not to scale.

stations.name: Goldstone
stations.text: Its largest antenna, Deep Space Station 14, is 230 feet (70 meters) across.
stations.alt: Illustration of a large dish antenna in a sandy, hilly landscape.

stations.name: Madrid
stations.text: Like every Deep Space Network site, it has one huge 230-foot (70-meter) antenna, one 85-foot (26-meter) antenna and multiple 112-foot (34-meter) antennas.
stations.alt: Illustration of a large dish antenna in a dry, rolling landscape.

stations.name: Canberra
stations.text: Among its antennas is Deep Space Station 35, a 112-foot-wide dish.
stations.alt: Illustration of a large dish antenna on a grassy plain.
